blocks.text: There are some who, thinking a mention of the locust out of place here, hold that חגב chagab in this passage is something else. For some of the Hebrews, interchanging Cheth and Ajin, חגב is the same as עגב, that is, the pudendum, as though it were meant that this part grows languid and slack in old men. Kimchi and Aben Ezra rightly reject this ^{(4)}. But for the latter חגב is הקרסול, the leg or the ankle. And for the Chaldee [III, 338] interpreter it is the ankle-bone of the foot; he renders Solomon's words thus: ויתנפחון אסחורי רגליך, And the ankle-bones of your feet shall swell. Others: the ankles of your feet. But that אסחורי or אסחוירי are the ankle-bones of the feet I have learned from the Gloss on the Talmud, tractate Iebamoth ch. 12, fol. 109 a, where אסחוירא is defined as קבילא המפסקת בין שוק לרגל, the ankle-bone dividing the leg from the foot. קבילא is not a Hebrew word, as people think, but the French cheville, which means the ankle-bone of the foot. For the one who uses it, R. Selomo, was a Frenchman. Again in tractate Menachoth fol. 33 a, we read that it is מקום חבור השוק והרגל הוי השוק זקוף מלמעלי והרגל שוכב בזה, the place where the leg joins the foot, namely with the leg raised above and the foot lying below. Hence אסחורא is often used by the Chaldee paraphrast for a step. And it corresponds to the Hebrew אשור, from which I would say it was derived, if the Chaldeans changed the Hebrew ש into ס, as the Arabs are accustomed to do. Now, to say what I think, I side with those for whom חגב chagab in this passage is not the locust but a part of the leg, inasmuch as the term leg also includes the thigh. And which part that is I think I have learned from the Arabs, for whom حجبة [ḥajaba] chagaba is the head of the thigh-bone. Golius: حجبة [ḥajaba] (Chagaba), the head of the hip, projecting on either side; the two are called حجبتان [ḥajabatān] chagabathani. Giggeius: الحجبتان [al-ḥajabatān] (Alchagabathan), each extremity of the thigh-bone and of the haunch above the groin. I understand the twin head of the thigh-bone, on account of which anatomists call it ἀμφικέφαλον [amphikephalon]. Since the movement of the leg begins from this head of the thigh-bone, Solomon rightly says of the old man, ויסתבל חגב, And the chagab grows heavy, to show that his gait is heavier and slower ^{(5)}.

The other passage is in chapter nine of the Apocalypse, which deals with locusts that have some features taken from the description of the real locust. But you may see many peculiar features added to these, which pertain to the mystery. To the former I assign the fact that [col. 495] smoke casts these locusts down onto the earth. For smoke rises from the pit of the abyss, ὡς καπνὸς καμίνου μεγάλης [hōs kapnos kaminou megalēs], as the smoke of a great furnace, or, as others read, καιομένης [kaiomenēs], of a burning one; hence the Syriac ܐܝܟ ܬܢܢܐ ܕܐܬܘܢܐ, and the Arabic edited at Paris تنور ملتهب [tannūr multahib]. There follows: And the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit; and out of the smoke came locusts upon the earth. It is in exactly this way that [III, 339] the Acridophagi hunt locusts, of whom Agatharchides says: Καπνῷ δὲ ταύτας θηρῶσιν, ἐκ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐπὶ γῆν καταφέροντες· [Kapnō de tautas thērōsin, ek tou aeros epi gēn katapherontes] They hunt them with smoke, bringing them down out of the air onto the ground. And Strabo: Ἐν ταῖς χαράδραις δὲ ἐμβάλλοντες ὕλην καπνώδη, καὶ ὑφάψαντες μικρόν· ὑπερπετάμεναι γὰρ τὸν καπνὸν σκοτοῦνται, καὶ πίπτουσι. [En tais charadrais de emballontes hylēn kapnōdē, kai hyphapsantes mikron; hyperpetamenai gar ton kapnon skotountai, kai piptousi.] They throw smoky material into the ravines and set it alight; and the locusts, flying over, are blinded by the darkness the smoke spreads, and fall. Whoever wants more should read Diodorus, book 3, where a deep ravine is described, extending over many stadia and filled with kindled material, which is abundantly available in those parts: Ἐγειρομένου δὲ καπνοῦ πολλοῦ, καὶ δριμέος, αἱ μὲν ἀκρίδες ὑπερπετόμεναι τὴν χαράδραν, καὶ διὰ τὴν τοῦ καπνοῦ δριμύτητα πνιγόμεναι, καταπίπτουσιν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, ὀλίγον διαπετασθεῖσαι τόπον· [Egeiromenou de kapnou pollou, kai drimeos, hai men akrides hyperpetomenai tēn charadran, kai dia tēn tou kapnou drimytēta pnigomenai, katapiptousin epi tēn gēn, oligon diapetastheisai topon] When much acrid smoke has been raised, the locusts, flying over the ravine and suffocated by the acridity of the smoke, fall to the ground after flying only a little way past that spot. The sacred writer seems to have alluded to this account of the Acridophagi ^{(6)}. Likewise, the statement in verses 5 and 10 that they harm men for five months seems to be made because locusts, born in spring, die toward the end of summer and do not usually live beyond five months. And their description in verse 7 as like horses prepared for battle is taken from Ioelis II, 4. Their appearance is as the appearance of horses, and like horsemen they shall run. And in verse 8, Their teeth were as the teeth of lions: so we have in Ioelis I, 6. His teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he has the molars of a lioness. But also the statement in verse 9, They also had breastplates, as it were breastplates of iron, pertains in some way to the nature of locusts, of which Claudian says:
— — a covering grown with it hardens on its back; nature has armed its skin. — —
